routes.description: Establish reflective Christianity as credible through a cumulative case from philosophical reasoning, scriptural and experiential considerations, and resurrection evidence, while limiting skeptical inferences from evil, disagreement, expert dissent, and Christian moral failure.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the positive considerations provide reasonable warrant for Christianity and the negative considerations neither render its core claims unlikely nor defeat the cumulative case when assessed together.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative positive case and the answers to skeptical objections to the conclusion that reflective Christianity remains credible.

centralBridges.description: Show that philosophical arguments can provide discriminating support for theism despite uncertainty about premises, divine motivations, and evidential partitioning.
Show that revelation, religious experience, and resurrection considerations supply warrant for distinctively Christian claims rather than generic theism alone.
Show that evil, religious disagreement, expert dissent, and moral failure do not outweigh or defeat the positive cumulative case.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify when cognitive limits and consequential complexity legitimately restrict skeptical likelihood judgments without indiscriminately defeating positive arguments.
Distinguish reasonable Christian credibility from certainty and explain why acknowledged disagreement need not require an atheistic conclusion.

routes.description: Establish skeptical atheism by challenging the predictive and explanatory force of the positive Christian considerations and presenting evil, religious disagreement, expert dissent, and Christian moral failure as cumulative evidence against Christianity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the positive arguments fail to make Christianity sufficiently probable and the negative considerations are better expected without the Christian account of God, revelation, resurrection, and transformation.

motionBridge.description: Connect the failure of the positive case and the cumulative skeptical evidence to the conclusion that Christianity is unlikely.

centralBridges.description: Show that philosophical arguments, biblical beauty, religious experience, and resurrection evidence lack the claimed discriminatory or explanatory force.
Show that apparently preventable suffering and persistent religious confusion are less expected under the proposed Christian God than under naturalism.
Show that informed dissent and the observed moral record materially reduce confidence in Christianity's truth and transformative claims.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply naturalistic explanations for fine-tuning and resurrection data that avoid disputed assumptions about divine psychology or miraculous intervention.
Require consistent treatment of uncertainty, cognitive limitation, comparative expertise, and likelihood reasoning across positive and negative arguments.

sections.title: Philosophical Arguments, Fine-Tuning, and Divine Psychology
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether philosophical and fine-tuning arguments predict a life-permitting universe under theism or instead depend on uncertain premises, contested value theories, and arbitrary evidential partitions.

sections.title: Scripture, Religious Experience, and Reflective Warrant
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether biblical qualities and religious experience distinguish Christian revelation and justify reflective belief despite rival experiences, counterarguments, and disagreement.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Naturalistic Explanation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether physical resurrection best explains the burial, appearances, and resulting bodily-resurrection belief or whether a naturalistic sequence explains the same evidence.

sections.title: Evil, Religious Disagreement, and Epistemic Limitation
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on whether suffering and failed or uneven revelation are improbable under Christianity, and whether appeals to consequential complexity or cognitive limits answer those inferences consistently.

sections.title: Expert Dissent, Rational Confidence, and Christian Moral Fruit
sections.rationale: This issue examines how interdisciplinary and specialist disagreement should constrain confidence and whether Christianity's claimed moral transformation generates unmet observable expectations relevant to credibility.
